title: Before You Ask What's Wrong With Your Child
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Kevin Stinehart reframes common parenting concerns by introducing the concept of 'under-practiced' children—kids who struggle behaviorally not because something is fundamentally wrong with them, but because modern life has deprived them of the repeated lived experiences needed to build self-regulation, social confidence, and independence. Rather than defaulting to the question 'What is wrong with my child?', Stinehart invites parents to ask: 'What has this child had enough chances to practice?' Children build self-regulation through repeated encounters with frustration, waiting, disappointment, and recovery—not through adult instruction to calm down. Social confidence comes through genuine peer experience: entering groups without adult arrangement, misunderstanding each other, repairing harm, being excluded, including others. Modern children often face less free play, less boredom, less responsibility, less manageable risk, and fewer chances to solve problems without adults immediately smoothing the road. Stinehart carefully carves out genuine clinical concerns (trauma, disability, severe anxiety, abuse) that require qualified professional support, positioning the 'under-practiced' frame as a first question rather than a replacement for real help. He introduces The Childhood Inputs Interview Workbook as a practical parent-child tool.
points: * The 'under-practiced' framework reinterprets behavioral struggles as missing developmental inputs rather than character flaws or disorders—changing the adult posture from tightening control to finding the missing practice field. * Children build self-regulation through repeated lived experiences with frustration, waiting, disappointment, and recovery—not through enough adult explanations about how to manage emotions. * Social confidence develops through real, unmediated peer experience: entering groups without adult arrangement, misunderstanding each other, repairing harm, being excluded, and trying again. * Modern children face reduced free play, less boredom, less responsibility, less manageable risk, and fewer chances to solve ordinary problems independently—creating a thinner developmental world. * The frame is not a substitute for genuine clinical concerns; trauma, disability, severe anxiety, abuse, and mental health issues require swift, appropriate professional support.
quotes: Children do not build self-regulation because adults tell them to calm down enough times. They build it through repeated lived experiences with frustration, waiting, disappointment, excitement, repair, movement, and recovery.
A lot of what we call behavior is the visible edge of a thinner developmental world.
If I think my child is simply being difficult, I tighten control. If I think my child may be under-practiced, I start looking for the missing practice field.

Modern children often have less free play, less neighborhood life, less outdoor time, less boredom, less responsibility, less mixed-age peer culture, less movement, less manageable risk, less community, and fewer chances to solve ordinary problems without adults immediately smoothing the road.
Then we ask them to walk into homes, classrooms, teams, places of worship, restaurants, and birthday parties and show capacities they may not have had enough chances to build.
